medium.conteudo_html:
I built Incident Rehearsal to explore service dependencies, estimate blast radius, and connect fault records with distributed-trace evidence — without confusing a possible connection with a confirmed root cause.

A service goes down.

An alert fires.

The logs show errors, and the team starts investigating.

But identifying the service that failed is only the beginning.

Which other services depend on it? What changed recently? Is there a previous incident worth examining? Which traces overlap with the fault? And what do we actually know, versus what are we only guessing?

These questions are difficult because the answers rarely live in one place. They depend on relationships between services, deployments, incidents, faults, traces, and spans.

That is the problem I wanted to explore during Graph Hacks by WeMakeDevs and FalkorDB.

I built Incident Rehearsal — Explainable AI Blast-Radius Investigator, a graph-powered prototype that helps developers investigate service dependencies and explore fault-related evidence.

Try it: Live Demo

Explore the code: GitHub Repository

The problem isn’t just finding data. It’s connecting it.

Imagine an application with several services:

  • A mobile API depends on checkout.
  • Checkout depends on authentication.
  • A cart service also depends on authentication.
  • Authentication depends on a user database.

Now imagine authentication starts failing.

Knowing that authentication is unhealthy is useful, but it doesn’t answer

the next question: which other parts of the application might be affected?

A developer needs to follow the dependency relationships and understand how far the impact could travel.

The same problem appears when investigating distributed traces. A fault record may identify a component and a time interval, while trace data contains spans, service mappings, timestamps, and parent-child relationships.

Looking at isolated records gives you pieces of the picture. Following their connections gives you a way to investigate the picture itself.

I wanted to build a tool where those relationships were part of the investigation, rather than just information displayed on a dashboard.

Why I chose FalkorDB

FalkorDB became the central data layer for Incident Rehearsal.

Instead of maintaining a static list of which services might be affected, I represented services and their relationships as a graph that the application could query.

For example, the synthetic demonstration graph uses nodes such as Service, Developer, Deployment, PastIncident, and Runbook.

The relationships describe how those entities connect:

  • DEPENDS_ON connects one service to another.
  • MAINTAINED_BY links a service to its developer.
  • DEPLOYED_TO connects a deployment to a service.
  • AFFECTED links a historical incident to a service.
  • DOCUMENTED_IN links a service to its runbook.

This allows the application to explore more than a single service record.

It can traverse dependency paths, retrieve related deployment and incident information, and connect the investigation with ownership and runbook context.

Here’s an example of the Cypher query used to explore dependent services:

MATCH p = (dependent:Service)-[:DEPENDS_ON*1..5]->(target:Service)
WHERE target.name = $service_name
RETURN p, length(p) AS hops
ORDER BY hops, dependent.name

The important part is the relationship traversal.

The query follows paths through DEPENDS_ON relationships and returns the paths and their lengths. The selected service name is passed as a parameter rather than being inserted directly into the query text.

If the target is AuthService, the graph can reveal dependent paths through Checkout and MobileAPI, as well as the direct dependency from CartService.

This makes the dependency structure queryable instead of relying on a manually prepared list.

Two investigation workflows, with different purposes

One design decision was especially important: I kept the synthetic demonstration graph separate from the research graph.

They serve different purposes, and merging them would make it easier to confuse hypothetical examples with experimental evidence.

1. Incident Rehearsal: Exploring a service’s blast radius

The first workflow uses a small synthetic application architecture containing five fictional services:

MobileAPI, Checkout, CartService, AuthService, and UserDB.

The application lets you focus on a service and explore its dependency relationships, health information, deployments, historical incidents, ownership, and runbook context.

It also includes a deterministic rehearsal workflow.

Instead of only showing which services are connected, the workflow compares reachability before and after removing a candidate incoming dependency edge from an in-memory copy of the graph. It can compare candidate edges and rank them by the number of reachable services lost.

Why do this?

Because it gives developers a way to explore a hypothetical question: how would the dependency structure change if this connection were removed?

Importantly, this is a structural simulation. The application does not permanently delete a relationship from the stored graph to perform the comparison.

And because the service data is synthetic, the resulting blast radius is a demonstration of dependency analysis — not a measurement of impact on a real production system.

2. Murphy Research: Connecting faults with trace evidence

The second workflow investigates a bounded sample of experimental fault-injection and distributed-tracing data.

I used the Murphy traces dataset associated with the DeathStarBench hotel-reserv benchmark.

For the current pilot, I imported:

  • 1 research dataset and 1 research run
  • 6 recorded fault events
  • 4 unique research components
  • 5 traces
  • 55 spans

The stored graph also contains six recorded research services and 17 parent-child span relationships.

The research graph uses its own labels and relationships, including FaultInjection, ResearchTrace, ResearchSpan, ResearchService, HAS_FAULT, HAS_TRACE, HAS_SPAN, and PARENT_OF.

When a fault is selected, the application examines traces and spans whose stored Jaeger timestamps overlap the selected fault’s time interval. It presents details such as trace IDs, span IDs, services, operations, source files, and explicit parent-child evidence.

The application also renders a trace-topology view using the recorded service mappings and parent-child span relationships.

I deliberately avoided inventing connections when the available data could not justify them.

That led to one of the most important distinctions in the project:

A trace overlapping a fault is evidence worth investigating. It is not proof that the fault caused the trace’s behavior.

Temporal overlap helps narrow the investigation. It does not establish causation by itself.

The current pilot is also limited to its imported sample. I have not imported the dataset’s Prometheus metrics or wrkOutput, so this version does not detect CPU or memory anomalies from those sources or claim measured production impact.

You can find the dataset through the University of Illinois Data Bank record.

Where the AI agent fits

Incident Rehearsal uses Python and Streamlit for the application, FalkorDB for graph storage and traversal, and LangChain with Google Gemini for the AI-assisted synthetic incident-report workflow.

I didn’t want the language model to invent an investigation from a vague description of an error.

Instead, the application exposes defined graph-backed tools that retrieve relevant information. The agent can use those results to help prepare an investigation report.

The report workflow is instructed to distinguish between:

  • Facts retrieved from the graph
  • Observations reported by the user
  • Hypotheses that still need investigation
  • Information that remains unknown

That distinction matters because a confident explanation can still be wrong.

The AI-assisted report workflow also has a deterministic graph-tool fallback for detected Gemini quota exhaustion.

The Murphy Research workflow is different: its selected-fault analysis is deterministic and graph-backed. It does not require an LLM call to determine timestamp overlap or display recorded trace relationships.

Separating these responsibilities makes the current behavior easier to inspect and explain.

Three engineering decisions I wanted to get right

1. Keep graph access predictable

The investigation tools use parameterized, read-oriented FalkorDB queries through graph.ro_query(...).

The ordinary investigation workflow reads the stored evidence; it doesn’t need unrestricted write access to explore an incident.

The research importer also defaults to dry-run mode and only writes when explicitly instructed to do so. The synthetic graph is seeded separately.

These boundaries make the data flow easier to understand and reduce the chance of an investigation unexpectedly changing the evidence it is examining.

2. Keep synthetic and research data separate

The synthetic graph is designed to demonstrate service dependencies and hypothetical scenarios.

The research graph represents a bounded sample of experimental records.

They should not be treated as interchangeable.

Keeping them separate preserves the meaning and provenance of the evidence and makes it clear which results are illustrative and which come from recorded research data.

3. Show what is known — and what isn’t

Incident investigation involves uncertainty.

A missing parent span is not the same as evidence that no parent existed. An unresolved target identity should remain unresolved. A timestamp that is unavailable should not be silently guessed.

I wanted the application to preserve these distinctions rather than filling every gap with an apparently complete diagram or a confident AI-generated explanation.

For an investigation tool, being explicit about uncertainty is a feature, not a weakness.

What building this project taught me

The first lesson was that a graph database should do real work.

For this project, FalkorDB is not simply a place to store information or a graph visualization drawn over another system. Dependency traversal, blast-radius analysis, fault-to-component relationships, trace membership, and parent-child span evidence are central to what the application does.

The graph is part of the investigation logic itself.

The second lesson was that an AI agent and a graph database solve different parts of the problem.

The graph makes relationships explicit and queryable. Deterministic tools retrieve the evidence. The language model can help turn some of that evidence into a readable report.

I don’t need the LLM to rediscover relationships that can be queried directly.

The third lesson was that explainability requires more than a generated explanation.

Showing a sentence that says a service might be affected is not enough. I want the developer to be able to inspect the dependency path, the records, and the relationships behind that conclusion.

Finally, I learned how important scope is when building a prototype.

It would be easy to describe this project as a system that automatically finds root causes. But that would overstate what the current implementation demonstrates.

The synthetic workflow explores structural blast radius. The research workflow examines a bounded collection of recorded faults and trace evidence. Neither establishes a confirmed root cause in a live production system.

Being precise about that boundary makes the project more useful, not less.

What comes next?

There are several things I would like to improve.

First, I want to broaden the research sample and evaluate the investigation workflow against more fault scenarios.

Second, I want to explore importing additional metrics with clear provenance so that the application can investigate more than timestamp overlap and trace structure.

Third, I want to improve how the final report connects each statement to the evidence supporting it, making it easier for a developer to move from a summary to the underlying graph relationships.

I’d also like to test whether this workflow genuinely helps developers narrow down their next investigative step compared with inspecting the same evidence manually.

Those are future directions, not capabilities I am claiming the current prototype already has.

Try Incident Rehearsal

Incident Rehearsal is my project for Graph Hacks: Give Your AI Agents Real Context, organized by WeMakeDevs with FalkorDB.

  • Live demo: https://incidentrehearsal.streamlit.app/
  • Source code and setup instructions: https://github.com/prithvi-yadav/Incident-Rehearsal-Explainable-AI-Blast-Radius-Investigator
  • Hackathon: https://www.wemakedevs.org/hackathons/falkordb
  • Research dataset: https://doi.org/10.13012/B2IDB-6641912_V1

My goal with this project was not to build another chatbot that explains an incident in convincing language.

It was to explore how connected data can give an investigation more structure: which services depend on which, which traces overlap a recorded fault, what relationships are actually present, and what still needs to be verified.

A graph won’t magically identify every root cause. An LLM won’t magically make incomplete evidence reliable.

But when the relationships are represented explicitly, the queries are constrained, and the limitations are visible, developers have a much better foundation for investigating what happened.

That is what I wanted to explore with Incident Rehearsal: not just an AI that gives an answer, but an investigation whose evidence can be followed.

medium.conteudo_html:
AI coding agents are getting remarkably good at implementing backend features. The dangerous part is how easily correct-looking code can violate the guarantees your production system depends on.

A backend engineer asks Claude Code to implement a new endpoint for updating customer billing information. The agent examines the existing Spring Boot project, identifies the relevant controller and service classes, generates a request DTO, adds validation annotations, writes a repository method, and produces a collection of tests that pass successfully. The implementation follows the project’s naming conventions, the code is reasonably clean, and the pull request looks like something an experienced developer could have written during an ordinary afternoon.

The engineer reviews the changes, notices no obvious problems, and approves the pull request. The feature reaches production, where it performs exactly as expected for most customers. Requests return successful responses, database records are updated, and the monitoring dashboard shows no unusual increase in errors or latency.

Several weeks later, the company discovers that users from one customer organization can modify billing records belonging to another organization by changing an identifier in the request.

The AI agent didn’t generate a syntax error, misunderstand the framework, or introduce a dependency that failed to compile. It implemented the requested functionality using a repository method that looked entirely reasonable. The tests passed because they verified successful updates and invalid request handling, but nobody had explicitly tested whether the authenticated user was authorized to modify the requested record.

This is a hypothetical scenario, but the failure mechanism is a familiar production security problem. An application can validate its inputs, authenticate its users, and still expose unauthorized access when object-level authorization is missing.

AI coding agents make this category of mistake particularly important because they can generate large amounts of plausible code faster than engineers can examine every assumption behind it.

The central challenge is deciding which production guarantees must be established before an AI-generated change can be trusted.

The First Problem Is That AI Agents Learn From the Codebase You Already Have

When engineers use Claude Code, Cursor, or similar AI coding tools, they often expect the agent to follow existing project conventions. This is one of the most useful capabilities of repository-aware coding assistance because it reduces the amount of context an engineer needs to explain manually.

The agent can inspect controllers, services, repositories, configuration files, and tests to infer how the application is organized. It may recognize the project’s dependency injection patterns, error-handling conventions, and preferred testing framework.

But the existing codebase isn’t necessarily a reliable description of the system’s security and correctness requirements.

Imagine a multi-tenant application where most repository methods include tenant identifiers in their queries. A few older methods, however, retrieve records using globally unique identifiers without explicitly verifying tenant ownership because they were originally used only by trusted internal services.

An AI agent implementing a new customer-facing endpoint may reuse one of those methods because its name and return type match the requested functionality.

The resulting code could compile successfully and appear consistent with the existing architecture while crossing an important security boundary.

The issue isn’t that the agent failed to imitate the codebase. It may have imitated the wrong part of it.

This is why production coding instructions need to distinguish between implementation conventions and mandatory engineering invariants.

A naming convention is a preference. Tenant isolation is a correctness and security requirement.

An agent should be guided to preserve the latter even when the surrounding code provides inconsistent examples.

Spring Boot Authorization Is More Than Checking Whether a User Is Logged In

Consider a simplified Spring Boot service that updates a billing record.

@Transactional
public BillingRecord updateBilling(
        UUID billingId,
        UpdateBillingRequest request) {

BillingRecord record = repository.findById(billingId)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException("Billing record not found"));
    record.setBillingEmail(request.billingEmail());
    return record;
}

The method is straightforward, and its behavior is easy to test. Given an existing billing record and a valid email address, it updates the entity inside a transaction.

The problem is that the method says nothing about whether the caller is authorized to modify the record.

Authentication elsewhere in the application doesn’t automatically solve this problem. Knowing which user submitted the request is different from establishing that the user has permission to modify a particular object.

A safer design requires a trusted authorization context and an explicit ownership or permission check. Depending on the application’s architecture, that might involve a tenant-scoped repository query combined with an authorization policy that verifies the user’s role and permitted operations.

For example, a repository method could retrieve the record using both its identifier and the tenant identifier derived from the authenticated principal.

repository.findByIdAndTenantId(billingId, trustedTenantId)

The tenant identifier must come from a trusted server-side context rather than being accepted uncritically from the request body. Otherwise, an attacker could simply supply another tenant’s identifier and defeat the intended isolation.

Even this approach isn’t universally sufficient. Some applications support delegated administration, cross-tenant support operations, or fine-grained permissions that require additional authorization rules.

The important point is that the authorization model must be explicit.

If you ask an AI coding agent to create an endpoint without defining these requirements, it may implement a technically correct update operation that violates the application’s security boundaries.

The Second Problem Is That Passing Tests Can Create False Confidence

AI coding agents are increasingly capable of generating tests alongside their implementations. This can improve development speed, particularly when the tests exercise meaningful edge cases and verify behavior that would otherwise be overlooked.

But automatically generated tests often reflect the same assumptions as the implementation.

If an agent assumes that finding a billing record by its identifier is sufficient authorization, it may generate tests confirming that existing records can be updated and missing records return an appropriate error.

Those tests can pass without ever examining cross-tenant access.

The problem is especially serious when a pull request includes many tests because the apparent volume of coverage can create confidence that the implementation has been thoroughly validated.

Test quantity isn’t the same as test quality.

For a multi-tenant billing endpoint, meaningful tests should verify that an authorized user can update a permitted record, that an unauthorized user cannot modify another tenant’s record, and that failed authorization does not produce a database change.

The tests should also examine how the application handles invalid inputs and whether sensitive information appears in error responses.

If authorization depends on roles, the test suite needs to distinguish between roles that can view billing information and roles that can modify it.

These requirements should come from the application’s security model rather than from the code the agent happened to generate.

A useful AI-assisted workflow therefore begins by establishing the behaviors that must remain true, including behaviors the feature isn’t supposed to allow.

That changes the role of the tests. They become independent constraints against which the implementation is evaluated rather than a demonstration that the generated code behaves as its author expected.

The Third Problem Is That AI-Generated Transactions Can Be Correct Locally and Dangerous Globally

Security boundaries are only one category of production risk. Transaction handling introduces another set of problems that can be difficult to recognize through ordinary code review.

Suppose an AI agent implements a service that updates a customer subscription and sends a notification through an external API.

The generated method might use Spring’s @Transactional annotation to ensure that the database update occurs atomically.

Inside the transaction, the service saves the subscription and calls the notification provider.

At first glance, the implementation seems reasonable because the database work is protected by a transaction.

But the external notification call isn’t part of the database transaction.

If the notification provider accepts the request and the database transaction later rolls back, the customer may receive a message describing a subscription change that never committed.

If the external call times out, the application may not know whether the provider accepted it. Retrying without an appropriate operation identity could create duplicate notifications.

The reverse ordering has problems as well. Committing the database change before attempting notification avoids holding the transaction open during a network call, but a process crash between the two operations can leave the notification unsent.

A transactional outbox is one possible solution when the business requires durable coordination between database state and asynchronous publication. It allows the application to record the business change and an outgoing event within the same database transaction, after which a separate process delivers the event.

That design still requires careful handling of duplicate delivery, retries, and consumer idempotency.

An AI agent can implement an outbox pattern, but it cannot determine the required business guarantees from the word @Transactional alone.

Engineers need to define whether notifications are best-effort, whether duplicate delivery is acceptable, and what recovery behavior the workflow requires.

Without those constraints, an agent can produce clean code that satisfies the immediate feature request while introducing failure modes that only become visible under production conditions.

The Fourth Problem Is That AI Agents Can Make Performance Regressions Look Like Ordinary Refactoring

Consider a Spring Boot endpoint that retrieves a list of customer orders and returns a response containing selected details about each order.

An AI agent may implement the endpoint by loading a page of orders and then accessing related entities while mapping each order into a response DTO.

The code can look perfectly natural.

return orders.stream()
    .map(order -> new OrderResponse(
        order.getId(),
        order.getCustomer().getName(),
        order.getItems().size()
    ))
    .toList();

Depending on the entity mappings, persistence context, and fetching strategy, accessing related data may trigger additional database queries.

If the endpoint returns hundreds of orders, the implementation could generate a large number of database operations instead of retrieving the necessary data through a controlled query strategy.

The agent may also generate a test using a small in-memory dataset that never exposes the problem.

Under production traffic, the endpoint can increase database load substantially even though the business logic is correct.

A meaningful review should examine query count, query shape, expected result size, and the behavior of lazy-loaded associations.

The appropriate solution might involve DTO projections, carefully chosen fetch joins, batching, or a dedicated read query. The correct approach depends on pagination requirements, cardinality, and the amount of data being retrieved.

For example, blindly applying a collection fetch join to a paginated query can introduce its own problems, including incorrect or inefficient pagination behavior.

This is why instructions such as “optimize the query” are insufficient.

A production-aware coding workflow should require evidence about the actual database behavior and should discourage introducing fetching strategies without considering their consequences.

The Fifth Problem Is That AI Agents Can Change More Than You Intended

Modern coding agents can inspect a repository, modify multiple files, run commands, and iterate on their implementation. That capability makes them useful for changes that would otherwise require repetitive manual work.

It also expands the scope of potential mistakes.

Suppose you ask an agent to add a new customer export feature. During implementation, it modifies a shared serialization utility, changes an existing configuration default, and updates a common dependency because those changes make its generated code easier to integrate.

The feature works, but the pull request now affects unrelated application behavior.

A shared serialization change could alter API responses consumed by other services. A configuration update could affect production resource limits. A dependency upgrade could introduce compatibility changes that aren’t covered by the feature’s tests.

The agent may have good reasons for making each modification, but those reasons need to be examined.

Production code review should distinguish changes required for the requested behavior from opportunistic refactoring and unrelated infrastructure modifications.

This doesn’t mean every pull request must be artificially small. Some features genuinely require coordinated changes across several components.

But the scope should be intentional.

An effective AI coding workflow asks the agent to identify its planned modifications, explain why shared components need to change, and avoid expanding the task without explicit approval.

For sensitive repositories, command execution and deployment permissions should also be restricted independently of the instructions given to the model.

A prompt telling an agent to be careful is not a substitute for repository permissions, credential isolation, and approval controls.

Production Guardrails Should Be Verifiable, Not Inspirational

Many teams begin introducing AI coding standards with broad statements about code quality.

They tell agents to follow best practices, write secure code, avoid unnecessary complexity, and ensure that changes are production-ready.

Those instructions sound responsible, but they leave too much room for interpretation.

A more useful approach defines concrete constraints that can be reviewed or tested.

For a multi-tenant backend, that might mean requiring tenant-scoped access to customer-owned data and explicit authorization checks for sensitive operations.

For database changes, it could mean requiring migration compatibility with currently deployed application versions and prohibiting destructive schema operations without a separately reviewed rollout plan.

For external side effects, it could mean requiring explicit retry semantics, operation identifiers where necessary, and documented behavior when the outcome of a network request is uncertain.

For performance-sensitive endpoints, it might mean reviewing query count, bounded result sizes, and the expected behavior under realistic production workloads.

These constraints are useful because they describe observable properties of the system.

An engineer can inspect the implementation, write tests, or run appropriate analysis to determine whether the requirement has been satisfied.

The agent can also use them while planning its implementation, but the final verification should remain independent of the agent’s own claims.

The purpose of guardrails is to make important engineering assumptions visible before code reaches production.

A Practical Claude Code or Cursor Production Review Workflow

A useful AI-assisted development workflow begins before code generation.

The engineer defines the requested behavior, the relevant business constraints, and the production guarantees that the implementation must preserve. This includes identifying security boundaries, transactional requirements, compatibility expectations, and important failure scenarios.

The agent can then inspect the repository and propose an implementation plan.

Before accepting the plan, the engineer should examine whether the proposed changes affect shared components, data contracts, or operational behavior beyond the original request.

During implementation, automated checks should provide independent feedback. Depending on the project, these may include compilation, unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, dependency scanning, and security-focused test cases.

For changes involving databases, concurrency, or external services, additional validation may be necessary.

A repository-level test suite can verify functional behavior while still missing race conditions, unexpected query amplification, or failures caused by real dependency behavior.

Those risks may require targeted integration tests, concurrency tests, realistic load testing, or controlled failure injection.

Before merging, the reviewer should inspect the final diff rather than relying on the agent’s summary. The summary can help navigate the changes, but it shouldn’t replace verification of the code that will actually be deployed.

Finally, production rollout controls should reflect the risk of the change.

A low-risk internal formatting adjustment doesn’t need the same release process as an authorization change affecting customer billing records.

High-impact changes may require gradual rollout, additional monitoring, or a documented recovery procedure.

The goal is to use AI to accelerate implementation without allowing implementation speed to determine the organization’s acceptable level of risk.

AI Coding Tools Change the Economics of Backend Engineering

The most important change introduced by AI coding agents is that producing code is becoming less expensive relative to understanding its consequences.

A developer can now generate controllers, services, tests, configuration files, and database migrations in a fraction of the time previously required for manual implementation.

That creates opportunities for faster delivery, but it also changes where engineering effort should be concentrated.

When implementation becomes easier, teams may approve larger changes more frequently. Reviewers can become overloaded, and the volume of plausible code can make it harder to identify the few assumptions that determine whether a change is safe.

The organization may begin shipping faster while accumulating risks that aren’t visible through ordinary functional tests.

Senior engineers need to respond by strengthening the practices that validate correctness, security, and operational behavior.

That includes defining architectural boundaries, establishing reliable automated checks, and making high-risk changes easier to identify during review.

It also requires understanding where AI assistance is appropriate and where additional human scrutiny is necessary.

An agent can help generate a database migration, but the engineer remains responsible for understanding whether it can be deployed safely alongside existing application versions.

An agent can propose a retry policy, but someone must determine whether repeating the operation is safe.

An agent can implement an authorization check, but the organization must define the policy that the check is supposed to enforce.

The faster code can be generated, the more valuable those decisions become.

The Real Risk Isn’t That AI Writes Bad Code

Poor code is often easy to recognize. It may fail compilation, violate obvious project conventions, or produce incorrect results during ordinary tests.

The more difficult risk is code that looks professional, passes its tests, and satisfies the visible feature request while violating an unstated production requirement.

A missing tenant boundary may remain invisible until someone attempts unauthorized access. An unsafe retry may appear only after a network timeout. A database performance regression may remain hidden until the endpoint processes realistic production data.

These failures are dangerous because they can survive the development workflow without creating obvious warning signs.

Claude Code and Cursor can be valuable engineering tools, but their output needs to be evaluated against requirements that are independent of the generated implementation.

The objective isn’t to slow every change down or require engineers to distrust every line of AI-generated code.

It’s to establish a development process where the most consequential risks are identified deliberately rather than discovered by customers after deployment.

That is a more useful definition of production readiness than whether an AI agent can produce a working feature.

Give Your AI Coding Agent Better Production Constraints

I created AI Backend Production Safety Coding Guardrails for Claude Code, Cursor & Codex for backend engineers who want to approach AI-assisted development with clearer production engineering constraints.

The resource focuses on the engineering judgment required when AI-generated changes affect backend correctness, reliability, security, and maintainability. It’s intended to help engineers think beyond whether generated code compiles and consider the production consequences of accepting it.

If you’re using coding agents to modify Spring Boot services, database access, asynchronous workflows, or other backend components, the important question is whether your review process consistently examines the risks that matter.

A structured set of guardrails can help make those expectations more explicit, although it doesn’t replace testing, code review, security controls, or professional engineering judgment.

medium.titulo: how to build AI products from scratch with Claude Code (steal this)
medium.resumo: if Claude knows every answer about the product you’re building and you don’t.. then you don’t really have control over what you’re…
medium.conteudo_html:
if Claude knows every answer about the product you’re building and you don’t.. then you don’t really have control over what you’re building. that’s the basic rule of software engineering you are missing.

when we wrote the code yourself back then, we at least had to think through those things.

because software engineering was never supposed to be just writing code anyway. you’re using software to solve a business problem. and if you’re building the whole product with AI, you need to be even clearer about what that problem is and what you’re actually asking it to build.

in this blog i will share my own process i follow to build production apps with Claude/Codex, which helped me deliver products worth over $10k.

1. learn the domain before you write the scope

one thing i tell people is that domain knowledge should be part of your stack. sounds strange maybe, but it matters as much as knowing which framework or library to use.

knowing React or FastAPI won’t tell you how people actually do the work, who needs to see what, or what happens after somebody takes an action. you can build a beautiful screen and still make the actual work harder for people who will be using it.

so having an idea of how that work actually happens is a great context here. what do people do today? where do they get stuck? how do other similar domain products handle it? which parts make sense for this product and which don’t? talk through the domain until you can make a useful suggestion, not just repeat the client’s idea back to them.

if a client comes to you with a high-level idea, they may know what they want to sell. but they probably haven’t figured out every module, workflow, field and permission already. and i don’t think they should have to spend weeks sitting with an engineer to define each one. that’s part of the work you’re being trusted to do.

you do the R&D, come back with a proposed scope, and bring them the decisions that matter to their business. what needs to be in the first version? does the way they plan to sell it change how it should be deployed? they should decide those things with you.

when you’re building a product end to end, you end up wearing a few hats. a bit of product manager, requirements person, engineer, UI/UX person, tester, and the one thinking about deployment too. AI makes it possible to do more of this independently, and i’ve been working this way for a while. but it only works if you understand the problem well enough to make those decisions.

2. decide what you’re actually building

once you get enough idea of the domain, the next step is mapping the main user journeys. and i don’t mean just drawing what pages the frontend will have. you need to see the whole product from a 360 angle under one umbrella. what does the user do first? which module owns that action? what data gets created? who can see it later? what happens if the same action is tried twice?

this is where i write the main product requirements down. call it an SRS or a product requirements doc, whatever works for your project. it should cover the users, the core flows, functional requirements, constraints, and what success looks like. you don’t need to describe every button there. you need enough detail that somebody new can understand what the product is supposed to do without reading your old chats.

then divide the product into phases. what’s needed now for the core of the product, what can wait, and what are we explicitly not building? i mean out of scope. write down the reason too when it matters. cuz a new idea will come up in the middle of development. sometimes from you, sometimes from the client while reviewing. Claude can happily build it, even if it changes the timeline or the data model, unless you stop and decide where it belongs.

for each phase i want a few acceptance criteria. not just “we built a dashboard.” more like “a user can complete this flow with real data” or “a user from another customer account can’t access this record.” you can actually test those. then ask whether the flow made the user’s work easier too, because passing tests and solving the business problem are different things.

put the constraints here as well. some are business constraints, like how the client will sell or deploy the product. some are functional, like who can approve an action. some are architectural, like tenant isolation or an external system that might be unavailable. this is the stuff Claude should know before it starts deciding things on its own.

3. work out the data, architecture and UI before individual features

now you can start seeing the product as an actual system. first i draw a high-level picture of the modules and how information moves between them. then an ERD for the core data: the main tables, relationships, ownership, and the fields that matter to the first phase. not every future field has to be decided on day one, but if two modules depend on the same record, you should know which one owns it.

i also sketch the important screens and flows at this point. you can let Claude help with wireframes from the journeys and data model. but you still need to look at them as the user. is the important information visible together? will this person spend the whole day scrolling? what happens when the table is empty, the job is still running, or an action fails? this is where your domain research starts showing up in the UI.

then choose the stack based on how the product will actually be used and delivered. on-prem is a good example. if the client will install it in their own environment, packaging, updates, secrets, data ownership and what you ship to them all need to be discussed early. choosing Python versus another language by itself doesn’t solve source-code exposure. a Docker image makes deployment repeatable, but you still need to check what files go into that image and who can inspect it. [Docker’s image-layer docs](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/building-images/understanding-image-layers/) are useful here.

same with the database. don’t decide SQL or NoSQL because one is trending. look at how the records relate, what has to change together in a transaction, and the queries the screens will actually make. if you have users, roles, approvals and connected records, a relational database may be a very sensible starting point. if a part of the data is flexible, that still doesn’t automatically mean the whole product needs a different database.

and the background work. if an AI job can take minutes, it probably shouldn’t keep an HTTP request open. now you need to decide how jobs are queued, retried, tracked, and shown to the user. Redis with a worker can fit one kind of job. [RabbitMQ](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials) gives you message routing and acknowledgements when that is what the workflow needs. [Kafka](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/) is something to consider when you actually need a retained stream of events that different consumers read or replay. these are different problems na. you don’t move from one to the next just because the product got bigger.

decide the API conventions too. for example: how resources are named, how lists are paginated, what error shape the frontend gets, how auth and permissions are checked, and what happens when a client retries a write. if one feature returns a different response style from another, Claude may still make both screens work, but maintaining them becomes annoying. write down the pattern once and make new features follow it.

and yes, a design system. not only colors and buttons. the table patterns, forms, status labels, loading, empty and error states. bring references from other products, but tell Claude what in the reference works and why. “make this modern” can mean a hundred different things to it.

4. keep the decisions in the repo, not in your chat history

this is where spec-driven development started making a lot more sense to me. you can explain a feature to Claude in one chat, get working code, and two weeks later have no idea why it made that decision. a new chat knows even less. if the reasoning only lives in the conversation, it isn’t really part of the project.

so i keep the product requirements and phase plan in files. the architecture, ERD, API conventions, design system, testing rules, and deployment steps live there too. `CLAUDE.md` points the coding agent to those files. i also keep a current-state note: what is true today, what is unfinished, and which decision is still waiting on me. new session? read the repo first.

for a feature change i use [OpenSpec](https://openspec.dev/docs/schemas/spec-driven). it gives the change a proposal, spec, design and task list. in plain words: why are we doing this, what should happen, how will we build it, and what work is left? the product requirements doc covers the overall product. these smaller specs cover what one change adds or changes. both need to agree.

the important part is reviewing the spec before asking Claude to implement it. check the normal flow, permissions, failure cases and what is out of scope. if it made an assumption, correct it there. a spec isn’t valuable because it is long. it is valuable because it records the decisions the code should follow.

and keep it current. if the code changes but the spec stays behind, the next session will confidently read the wrong story. that’s a maintainability problem you created for yourself.

5. give Claude one clear piece of coding work

once the spec is agreed, i give Claude a bounded part of the product to build. the relevant flow, the files and patterns to follow, what it must not change, and what would prove the task is done. if it needs a new table, dependency or API contract that wasn’t in the design, it should bring that back instead of quietly adding it.

and be specific when you review. “improve the UI” is not useful feedback. which screen? what is hard to scan? which information should stay visible? if you want better error handling, which failure and what should the user see? the more exact you are, the less Claude has to guess.

then read the diff and try the feature yourself. does the frontend use the real API? are permissions checked on the backend? does the data belong to the correct customer? what happens if the background job fails halfway through? if you can’t explain the change after reviewing it, don’t move on just because the tests turned green.

6. don’t let new requests quietly rewrite the product

new ideas are normal. first see what the request changes: scope, user flow, database, API, UI, timeline, tests, maybe even deployment. discuss the important trade-off with the client, decide whether it is for now or later, then update the relevant docs and spec. after that Claude gets the task.

schema changes need more attention once there’s real data. a new column can affect old rows, frontend types, API responses, imports and permissions. decide what happens to existing records, how the migration runs, and whether old and new versions of the app need to work during the release. update the ERD, migration, code and tests together. if the decision will be hard to reverse later, write down why you made it.

this is how you keep control while the product changes. the model can suggest an approach, but it shouldn’t decide your product’s future just because it found a quick implementation.

7. test what matters, then deploy from written steps

you decide what needs to be proven. rules need unit tests. important flows need integration tests against the real database. in a multi-tenant platform, you need tests proving one customer can’t read or change another customer’s data. and the main journeys need an end-to-end check where the UI, API and database work together. still click through the product yourself too.

AI features need their own checks. keep a small set of real inputs and look at the outputs when you change a prompt or model. what happens on a bad answer, a timeout, or a provider failure? what does each run cost? if a human must approve an AI result, test that the system cannot skip that step. these questions matter more than just seeing a nice response once in a demo.

before a release, know the order: environment and secrets, backup, migrations, app and workers, smoke test, logs and failed jobs. write down what to do if the release goes wrong too. that’s why the runbook belongs in the project, not in your head or one old chat.

that’s basically the workflow. the code can be written by Claude or Codex. you still need to understand the domain, decide what should exist, tell the model exactly what is allowed, and verify that the product does the job. that’s the engineering part i want to keep in my hands.

medium.titulo: I Was Arrested for Guarding Too Much: A Trial About the Null Check That Never Fired
medium.resumo: The charge: three counts of over-guarding. The evidence: one ternary that had never run. I was not the hero of the trial that followed.
medium.conteudo_html:
The charge: three counts of over-guarding. The evidence: one ternary that had never run. I was not the hero of the trial that followed.

TL;DR A guard should test what can actually happen at that layer. If the view already guarantees a value is non-null, checking it again in the script adds no safety — it adds noise, hides the real contract, and quietly turns bugs into wrong output. The ruling: guard at the boundary, once. Let interior code trust it.

The Arrest

It happened over a schedule board. Two guards came for me — guards, yes, for a man who guards too much.

The charge: over-guarding. Three counts — which three, the paperwork didn’t say. The evidence bag held only one exhibit — a Vue computed property, three lines long, the ternary bagged separately:

const pickTechName = computed(() =>
  pickTarget.value ? trayTechName(pickTarget.value) : ''
//  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ this part
)

It names the technician shown in the click-to-place banner on our schedule board. It also, per the arresting officer, stands guard against a null that could never reach it — a doorman paid to open a door that never gets a visitor.

The charge sheet was signed by the prosecutor — a colleague who had read the diff:

“Why do we check for null here when the view already guarantees it?”

I had no answer ready. The prosecution cannot compel a defendant to testify — so taking the stand was my counsel’s last card: “The defense calls the defendant.” What follows is the transcript of my cross-examination.

Exhibit A: The scene of the alleged crime

The computed has exactly one reader in the entire codebase:

<div v-if="pickTarget">
  <span class="font-semibold">Placing "{{ pickTarget.title }}"</span>
  <span v-if="pickTarget.techId">
    — click an open hour on {{ pickTechName }}'s row
  </span>
</div>

Note the two v-ifs already standing at the door. The banner exists only while pickTarget does; the hint, only when that job actually has a technician — an unassigned job is a real state here, not an exception. The computed is only ever read inside that block — after both checks have already passed.

Cross-Examination, Round One

Prosecutor: Why is that ternary there?

Me: Because pickTarget starts as null. trayTechName(null) would throw — it reads job.techId off the argument. The guard prevents a crash.

Prosecutor: When is the computed evaluated?

Me: When it’s read.

Prosecutor: And it’s read where?

Me: Inside the v-if="pickTarget" block.

Prosecutor: So at the moment of evaluation, can pickTarget be null?

The court reporter stopped typing.

My counsel rose: “Objection — the question assumes facts that haven’t been established.”

Overruled. The fact was about to be established anyway. computed in Vue is lazy: the getter does not run at setup. It runs on first read — and the only read is inside a subtree that requires pickTarget to exist. By the time my guard could fire, the condition it tests is already guaranteed false.

My counsel leaned over and whispered: “They have a point. Sit tight — let me see what else we have.”

Cross-Examination, Round Two

Prosecutor: Very well. It’s redundant today. But isn’t it cheap insurance for the future? Someone might read it unguarded later.

Me: It’s one comparison. It costs nothing.

Prosecutor: I am not asking what it costs. I am asking what it communicates.

My counsel tried again: “Objection — counsel is testifying.”

Overruled. The prosecutor’s point stood.

That is the question I had been avoiding. A guard is not a neutral act. It is a claim. It says: “this value can be null at this point.” A reader arriving later now has to hunt for the scenario where that’s true — and there is none. I had invented a hypothetical future reader to justify a check with no failure mode today.

“Cheap” was never the argument. “Honest” was.

Recess: The Three Kinds of Guards

During the recess, my counsel and I put together a list to explain our defense. Every guard is one of three things:

  • Boundary guard — ask “can this outside data be wrong?” Belongs where data comes in from outside: reading localStorage, an API response, a form submission.
  • Invariant guard — ask “can my guess be wrong?” Lives inside, where it must shout if wrong: assert(items.length > 0) before indexing.
  • Redundant guard — ask “is it already known?” Belongs nowhere. Someone already answered: re-checking what the view already guarantees.

Same question at every layer — and only three answers: yes, never (and say it loudly), or already answered. Only the first two need a check.

A guard should test what can actually happen at that layer — not re-test what a neighbor already guarantees.

The prosecutor rose to answer our list. “This distinction is not just opinion. P2053R1, a C++ committee proposal by Rostislav Khlebnikov and John Lakos, draws the same line: a check is ‘defensive’ when its assumption is expected to always hold. Human input and remote clients violate assumptions — those need validation at the boundary, not in trusted interior code.”

(The full proposal, plus Lakos’s CppCon talk summary in plain HTML, cover the same ground.)

My counsel leaned toward me. “But what about spacecraft? A bit flipped by radiation can turn an impossible state into a real one — that’s why NASA votes outputs across triple-redundant avionics.”

The prosecutor nodded. “Warranted, there — hardware itself can corrupt state. But this is a Vue component, not flight-control software. The template reads this computed only after pickTarget passes its v-if. This ternary doesn't guard against physics; it repeats a software guarantee."

The Prosecution’s Case: Three Counts of Over-Guarding

When court resumed, the paperwork finally became specific. The prosecutor read out the three counts — and none of them concern performance.

Count one: it lies about the contract. The guard advertises a possibility that doesn’t exist, taxing every future reader with a search for a phantom — after validation, later inconsistency is an internal error and should hard-fail (Michael Belivanakis).

Count two: it masks real bugs. If the invariant ever does break, the guard substitutes '' and renders a slightly wrong UI — instead of throwing a stack trace that points straight at the culprit. John Lakos's CppCon talk summary puts it as near-consensus: "Most would agree that a well-implemented library should do something other than silently continue when a pre-condition violation is detected." The pithier form comes from a heavily upvoted Software Engineering Stack Exchange answer: "isn't the null check, it's the silent fail" — programmer errors are best dealt with by failing immediately and loudly.

Count three: it breeds. Once neither caller nor callee can say who owns the check, every layer starts checking “just in case” — and the codebase fills with guards that guard nothing. This one has the best citation, and it comes from the man who invented the alternative.

The Evidence: Precedent from 1988

My counsel rose once more — keeping his promise from Round One to see what else we had. “I went looking for precedent that might excuse a ‘just in case’ guard, Your Honor. What I found is older than my client — and it is not on our side. The defense offers no opinions. Only precedent.”

Bertrand Meyer’s Design by Contract — the contract theory behind Eiffel — rests on a rule he calls non-redundancy. In his own chapter on the subject, Meyer states it as an absolute rule:

“Either you have the condition in the require, or you have it in an if instruction in the body of the routine, but never in both."

And he names the cost: redundancy “accumulated over a large system” buries “islands of useful processing in oceans of error-checking code.”

The official Eiffel documentation states it operationally — “a routine body should never test for the precondition, since it is the client’s responsibility” — and records the counterintuitive payoff: “one can get more reliable software by having fewer explicit checks in the software text.”

And in “Applying Design by Contract” (IEEE Computer), Meyer dismantles the exact argument I made on the stand — the “just in case” guard:

“Adding possibly redundant code ‘just in case’ only contributes to the software’s complexity… The result of such blind checking is simply to introduce more software, hence more sources of things that could go wrong at execution time, hence the need for more checks, and so on ad infinitum.”

There it is: my “cheap insurance” answer, refuted in 1992 by the man who defined the contract. The court accepts the precedent. I had been arguing against case law I didn’t know existed.

The Defense’s Best Argument: “But what if a user edits localStorage?”

My counsel played his last card — our strongest argument. “What if a user opens devtools and hand-edits the stored JSON? Then the data genuinely can be wrong, and the guard is justified.”

It deserved a real answer rather than a shrug.

The threat model is wrong. A dispatcher at a small business is not going to open devtools and hand-edit a JSON blob. If your safety depends on that being unlikely, you have larger problems than a null check — Instil’s write-up is blunt that below the public boundary these checks are overhead meant for tests and review, not runtime guards.

And this is the part I got wrong: the real reasons storage needs care have nothing to do with attackers. They are mundane — an earlier version of the app wrote a different shape, the storage filled and the write silently died, two browser tabs raced to write the same key, a user cleared their browsing data. None of that justifies guards sprinkled through the app. All of it justifies one guard, at the read boundary, where bytes become objects.

So the objection doesn’t defeat the rule — it confirms it. Reading localStorage is a boundary: data coming in from outside the app's control. And boundaries are guarded once, at the edge.

The Court’s Finding: Where the Guard Belongs in Vue

Before the jury retired, the judge settled the one question the case actually turned on: in a Vue component, who owns the guarantee?

There is a twist specific to Vue worth entering into the record: the template is a boundary.

That is not just convention — it is design. Vue’s docs describe the single-file component as “colocating the view, logic and styling of a component” — one component, one shared contract. Which is why they live in one file: split them, and neither side sees the whole guarantee — how duplicate checks get born.

TheCodeForge’s guide to the classic Vue template crash explains why: “Templates don’t wait. That first render is where nearly every Cannot read properties of undefined is born.” Their fix is the same instinct: “fix at the data boundary in setup(), not with scattered guards in every template."

And the idiomatic Vue form is a container v-if — the pattern you already saw in Exhibit A. SoundsCode's lesson says it plainly: the condition narrows the type for everything in that subtree.

One condition. One owner. Compare that to sprinkling pickTarget?.title, pickTarget?.techId, and a ternary inside the computed — three checks, three places to drift, and no single line that states what is actually guaranteed.

One honest footnote, because a sharp reader will spot it: pickTarget is read a second time outside that subtree — :selected-job-id="pickTarget?.id || null", handed to the unscheduled tray, which is always mounted. That optional chain is not the same species of check, and it should stay. There, null is a legitimate value — the tray renders whether or not anything is picked, and the child's prop is typed to receive String | null. That is a boundary handoff, not a redundant guard.

The rule was never “never use ?.." It is "use it where the value can actually be absent" — and the taxonomy above discriminating between two reads of the same ref is exactly the point.

The Verdict

Guard at the boundary, once. Let interior code trust it. Where you can, structure the code so the invalid state is impossible; where you cannot, fail loudly rather than substituting a value.

The template’s v-if="pickTarget" is the owner. The computed should not re-litigate it. The corrected exhibit:

const pickTechName = computed(() => trayTechName(pickTarget.value))

If someone later reads it unguarded, it throws — loudly, at the exact line that is wrong. That is not a bug. That is the contract doing its job.

A fair objection: a throw during render can blank the page in production. It is still the better trade — a silent '' hides the defect forever; a throw surfaces it. "Fail loudly" was never "crash the customer." It means fail where you can see it: the console in development, and an error boundary in production — Vue's onErrorCaptured or app.config.errorHandler, which reports the bug and renders a real error state instead of a card full of blanks.

The rule is not “never guard.” It is “never silently substitute.”

The jury was out for twenty minutes. When they filed back in, the foreman read the verdict to the judge.

Guilty on all three counts. The guard is released from duty — it never worked a day in its life.

Closing Remarks

The lesson was never about null checks. It is that my first two answers were shaped like reasoning while being motivated reasoning — an instinct, then a hunt for justifications instead of facts. The prosecutor was right the entire time; the record only changed when I read the sources and noticed the check I had been defending had never once executed.

The sentence was lighter than I deserved: one deleted ternary, and a paragraph in the project’s decision log.

A guard that guards nothing is cheap.

Defending it in court is not.

Domingo | 18 de outubro de 2026

A Velocità anunciou sua tradicional Black Friday Run, que neste ano celebra os 30 anos da marca. A ação é simples: no dia 30 de outubro de 2026, cada quilômetro que você correr será convertido em 1% de desconto, com um limite máximo de 42%. Isso significa que, se você completar uma maratona (42,195 km), garante o desconto máximo para usar em qualquer produto da loja, exceto eletrônicos e itens da marca On Running. Para participar, é preciso se cadastrar previamente e seguir o regulamento, que envolve conectar sua conta do Strava. O link para inscrição e mais detalhes está disponível aqui.

Bate-papo sobre a Maratona de Curitiba

Diretamente da TS Summit 2026, conversamos com Arthur Trauczynski, co-CEO da Global Vita, sobre a organização da Maratona de Curitiba. A expectativa é de um “sold out” em breve, com a participação de 12 mil atletas já confirmados e um limite de até 17 mil, incluindo corredores de 20 países diferentes. A prova, que acontece em um único dia, deve ser dividida em dois dias a partir de 2027 para acomodar mais participantes. Este ano, a mudança não foi possível pois a data não coincidiu com um feriado prolongado, o que dificultaria o fechamento de estacionamentos de órgãos públicos necessários para a estrutura do evento.

Com um prêmio total de R$ 604 mil, a Maratona de Curitiba se destaca como uma das maiores premiações do Brasil e possui o Selo Permit Ouro da CBAt e o World Athletics Road Race Label, reforçando o foco na categoria de elite. A expectativa é que os recordes da prova, como o masculino que foi quebrado no ano passado, sejam superados novamente.

Em relação à sustentabilidade, a prova mantém a certificação “Aterro Zero” e realiza a compensação de carbono. A grande novidade deste ano é a camiseta do evento, desenvolvida em parceria com a Woom, feita com um tecido biodegradável. Graças a uma enzima aplicada ao material, a camiseta se decompõe em até três anos caso seja descartada em um aterro sanitário.

Maratona de Pernambuco 2027 lança camisetas

A Maratona Internacional de Pernambuco, marcada para os dias 4 e 5 de setembro de 2027, já apresentou as camisetas de sua próxima edição.
